title: Efficient Exploration of the Rashomon Set of Rule Set Models

problem.claim: A single rule set gives only a partial representation of a learning task, motivating exploration of near-optimal rule-set models.

gap.claim: Existing Rashomon-set exploration can require computationally challenging exhaustive search, while exhaustive enumeration may introduce unnecessary redundancy.

contributions.claim: The work proposes efficient methods for exploring the Rashomon set of rule-set models with or without exhaustive search.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly present the methods as the first efficient methods for exploring the Rashomon set of rule-set models with or without exhaustive search.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report extensive experiments demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed methods across a variety of scenarios.

narrative_sequence.summary: Simple rule sets remain useful for interpretable predictions and high-stakes decision making despite increasingly complex predictive models.
A single rule set provides only a partial representation of a learning task.
Rashomon-set exploration considers all near-optimal models.
Existing exhaustive approaches are computationally challenging and may produce unnecessary redundancy.
The work proposes efficient exhaustive and non-exhaustive exploration methods and reports experiments on their effectiveness.

source_observation.claim: Exhaustive enumeration of a model set can be computationally challenging and unnecessarily redundant.

interpretation.claim: Exploration methods may benefit from trading complete enumeration for representative sampling or size estimation when the application permits.

application.claim: For interpretable model analysis, consider efficient non-exhaustive exploration when a representative view or set-size estimate is sufficient.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish when representative sampling or size estimation is adequate for a specific application.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the proposed algorithms or their computational complexity.
The abstract does not identify the experimental datasets, baselines, metrics, or quantitative results.
